title: What I Learned During Fika Time
paragraphs: In the spring of 2025, I took part in a two-month clinical clerkship at Lund University in southern Sweden. Lund University is a university with a history and research record among the foremost in Europe, and this time I did my clerkship in the intensive care unit (ICU) and anesthesiology in the first month and in emergency medicine in the second month. Seeing the local medical setting up close, experiencing the differences in healthcare system and culture, and improving my own clinical and language skills was a valuable experience.

In the ICU, I accompanied a supervising doctor who was in charge of several critically ill patients, followed the patients' courses day by day, and learned about themes such as respiratory management, nutrition and sedation. Unlike student clerkships in Japan, opportunities to examine patients were limited, but by following the same patient every day I was able to observe how the patient's condition changed over time and how the medical staff made judgments in response. In anesthesiology I was present at orthopedic and general surgery operations and learned about anesthetic induction, postoperative management and conduction anesthesia. The doctors answered questions carefully, and besides knowledge of anesthesia I was able to hear a great deal about the Swedish healthcare system and characteristics of how they work.

In emergency medicine in the second month, I took part in the orthopedic, surgical and internal medicine teams on a day-by-day rotation. The first week was mainly observation, but from the second week I examined patients myself and was entrusted with taking histories, summarising physical findings and presenting to the doctors. I was in charge of two to three patients a day and sometimes experienced suturing and explaining results. I was sometimes bewildered by the language barrier and the difference in medical knowledge, but there were many occasions when the medical English and presentation training I had done beforehand in Japan was useful in practice, and I could feel myself growing day by day.

My impression was that the Swedish medical setting is calmer than Japan's and that they spend time on each patient. On the other hand, there were also many cases in which patients' waiting times were very long, and it made me think that the quality and efficiency of medical care are strongly influenced by national character and social systems. I was also impressed that in Sweden procedures such as tracheal intubation and maintenance of anesthesia are handled by nurse anesthetists who have received special training, and that doctors and nurses work in collaboration, each making use of their own expertise.

In daily life, the safety in Lund was very good, and getting around on foot or by bicycle was comfortable. Prices were high, so I mainly cooked for myself while also enjoying the local food culture. On weekends I visited Stockholm and Copenhagen and was able to experience the townscapes and culture of the Nordic countries. I also had many opportunities to interact with local students and take part in workshops for exchange students, and through the coffee break culture called Fika I felt firsthand how casual conversations and connections among medical staff and students deepen.

Through this study abroad, I feel that my language ability, medical knowledge and understanding of different cultures have all improved. At the same time, it became an opportunity to think deeply about what kind of doctor I will aim to be in the future. From now on, I would like to aim to be a clinician who contributes to Japanese medical care while holding an international outlook, and to value my daily learning.
